prompt.context: In Mexico, banks prefer not to lend money to hospitals and schools because if one of these institutions defaults, the bank worries that it will be seen as the one responsible for liquidating their assets. Our client currently owns several universities in Mexico and is evaluating whether an opportunity exists to start a bank that would lend money to his various universities.
prompt.question: The client has three questions he wants us to address: (1) Is there an opportunity to lend money to universities? (2) If an opportunity exists, how big is it? (3) How should he structure the bank?

clarifying_info.q: What is the population breakdown in Mexico by age group?
clarifying_info.a: 0–15 years old: 7 million; 15–30 years old: 6 million; 30–45 years old: 5 million

clarifying_info.q: How many universities are there in Mexico?
clarifying_info.a: 200 universities total, and we can assume they are all at full capacity

clarifying_info.q: What is Mexico's population growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: Close to zero — use zero for simplicity

clarifying_info.q: Can existing universities accommodate more students (e.g. part-time/full-time mix)?
How many universities does the client currently own?

framework: 1. Market sizing — estimate total students enrolled, derive demand for new university capacity
2. Competitive landscape — identify whether other banks or institutions currently serve university lending; understand why incumbents avoid it
3. Credit risk segmentation — categorize universities by risk profile to assess lending viability
4. Loan sizing — estimate how much capital a typical new university needs (construction + working capital until positive FCF)
5. Funding structure — identify capital sources for the bank itself
6. Recommendation — synthesize findings into a go/no-go and structural guidance

questions.prompt: How many students are currently enrolled in universities across Mexico, and how many students enter university each year?
questions.guidance: Break the population into age cohorts. Apply a realistic university enrollment rate to the 15–30 cohort (e.g. 25%) and a small rate to the 30–45 cohort (e.g. 2%). Sum to get total enrolled. With zero population growth, incremental annual students = total enrolled × 0% growth (but the casebook uses 1% as the interviewee's working assumption before being told to use zero). Key insight: 1.6M students / 200 universities = 8,000 students per school on average.

math.setup: Population by cohort × assumed enrollment rate = enrolled students per cohort; sum cohorts; divide by number of universities for average school size
steps: Incremental students per year (at 1% growth assumption) = 1.6M × 1% = 16,000
New schools needed per year = 16,000 / 8,000 = 2 new schools per year
math.answer: ~1.6 million students currently enrolled; ~8,000 per university; ~2 new universities needed per year (under a 1% growth assumption)

questions.prompt: How would you segment universities for credit-risk assessment?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies at least three meaningful segmentation criteria. The casebook highlights: (1) New greenfield school vs. new branch of an existing operating university — branches are lower risk because the parent already has a revenue stream; (2) Student cohort flow — a school where students are evenly distributed across years is more creditworthy than one with most students in final years and few in early years (revenue cliff risk); (3) Geography — population growth and demand are uneven across Mexico; some regions may have no growth or oversupply.

questions.prompt: How would you estimate how much capital a typical new university would need?
questions.guidance: Two cost streams: (1) Capital expenditure — land acquisition, construction of buildings, equipment; (2) Working capital / operating losses — funding the school from opening until it reaches positive free cash flow (ramping enrollment means early years have high fixed costs and low tuition revenue). Best approach is to leverage the client's own data from his 15 existing universities to benchmark both cost categories rather than estimating from scratch.

questions.prompt: How would you fund the bank itself?
questions.guidance: Identify multiple capital sources: (1) Multilateral/supranational organizations such as the World Bank or IDB that have education-sector mandates; (2) The Mexican government, which may subsidize private universities offering programs not available through public institutions; (3) Commercial bank partnerships — large banks may not want to enter this niche alone but may co-invest with a specialist who understands the sector.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you consider when segmenting universities for credit scoring and lending risk?

categories.name: Entity type
ideas: New greenfield school vs. branch of an existing university system
Private vs. public university (public may have government backstop)

categories.name: Student demand / revenue stability
ideas: Even cohort distribution across all years (low revenue-cliff risk)
Program mix — vocational vs. degree programs, demand durability

categories.name: Geography
ideas: Urban vs. rural location (enrollment catchment size)
Regions with population growth vs. stagnant/declining areas
Competitive density — number of other universities in the area

categories.name: Financial health
ideas: Existing debt levels and debt-service capacity
Tuition pricing power relative to local income levels
Diversified revenue (research grants, corporate partnerships, housing)

categories.name: Operational factors
ideas: Track record of the owning entity (e.g., the client's 15 existing schools)

recommendation: There appears to be a genuine opportunity: Mexico's universities are at full capacity, population is growing, and no bank currently serves this lending niche, creating an unmet financing need

The immediate quantifiable demand is approximately 2 new university campuses per year, each requiring significant capital for land, construction, and ramp-up funding — a manageable, recurring deal flow for a specialist lender
The client's existing 15-university portfolio provides proprietary benchmarking data on costs and cash flow curves, giving him an information advantage over any potential competitor
risks: Regulatory/political risk: if a university defaults, the bank may face reputational and legal pressure not to foreclose, limiting recovery on collateral — this is exactly the fear that keeps incumbents out
Concentration risk: lending primarily to universities in one country creates sector and geographic concentration
Demand uncertainty: the 1% population growth assumption is critical; zero or negative growth eliminates the expansion thesis
next_steps: Conduct detailed due diligence on cost structure using client's 15 existing universities to build a reliable loan-sizing model
Engage with multilateral lenders (World Bank, IDB) and the Mexican government to explore co-lending or guarantee structures that mitigate default/recovery risk
Design a credit-scoring framework based on the segmentation criteria (entity type, cohort flow, geography) before approving any loans
Pilot with 1–2 loans to affiliated universities before scaling to third-party institutions
